Fernand Braudel was a French historian, born in 1902, who wrote the history of trade, markets and everyday life on the largest scale. He led the Annales school, which looked past kings and battles to geography, prices and the slow habits of ordinary people.

  • The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II (1949) was drafted largely from memory while he was a prisoner of war in Germany. It split time into three speeds: the near-still time of mountains and seas, the slow swings of economies and societies, and the quick time of events.
  • Civilization and Capitalism, 15th to 18th Century (three volumes, 1979) set out the ideas many pages here lean on.

In that work he saw three floors. At the bottom is material life: food, houses, tools. Above it is the open market of fairs and market towns. At the top is capitalism, the world of big merchants and bankers who sought monopoly. He also argued that each era's world economy had one leading city at its centre: Venice, then Antwerp, Genoa, Amsterdam and finally London. He called an exchange like the Amsterdam Exchange a fair that never closes. He died in 1985.
